candidates.name: Compliance tracker for private placement services (SPP) and the companies that use them

candidates.unchecked: Quarterly report format, deadline and filing channel. Whether an agrément fee or renewal cycle exists. Whether the closed agencies leave enough paying buyers. Willingness to pay of a fragile, partly informal group. Whether the user-company side (large firms) is out of scope.

candidates.unchecked: Current ARSP enforcement and filing process. Scope uncertainty by sector. Fee rates and periodicity. Overlap with K03 (copper-belt subcontractors). Not verified from a primary source.

coverage.found: Kinshasa launched mass road checks on 26 Jan 2026 (licence, technical inspection, vignette, transport authorisation, insurance) and public transport shrank. coverage.category: 19. Market traders, street vendors, money changers

coverage.category: 20. Small licensed premises with inspections: tattoo studios, driving schools, childminders and nurseries, small food producers, hunting outfitters
coverage.found: Nothing DRC-specific found for driving schools, nurseries or food producers. Unverified.

coverage.found: One search. No DRC text on station or distributor declaration duties found. Only a Feb 2026 AllAfrica item: the Hydrocarbons minister announced withdrawal of approvals for clandestine fuel depots in Kinshasa after a fire in Limete (enforcement signal, no register or duty identified). Nothing buildable confirmed.

coverage.category: 22. Grain, coffee, cocoa and other commodity traders, millers and warehouses
coverage.found: One search. The EU deforestation regulation (EUDR) is a generic exposure for coffee and cocoa exporters; sources conflict on dates and none mention DRC-specific OCC or agrément steps. Small exporters and cooperatives lack traceability data (AVSF note). No DRC-specific register found. See candidate on EUDR (unverified).

coverage.category: 23. Co-operatives, credit unions and savings groups
coverage.found: COOPEC/microfinance: the search found no BCC instruction or reporting rule (nothing verifiable). Mining cooperatives are mandatory structures for artisanal diggers; SAEMAPE identified cooperatives in Lualaba on 31 Jan 2026 and diggers at Kasulo from 4 Apr 2026 (see candidate, related to K07).

coverage.category: 24. Private clinics, labs and other health providers that bill insurers or state schemes
coverage.found: One search. No functioning compulsory health insurance scheme or insurer-billing workflow found for private clinics. SONAS is mentioned only in old theses. Mutuelle coverage was about 0.3% of the population in a 2009 figure. Nothing buildable on billing. A provincial licensing crackdown in Kinshasa is listed under category 35.

coverage.category: 25. Pharmacies, medicine importers, and users of controlled chemicals or precursors
coverage.found: Nothing new beyond K04 (ACOREP). Adds context: the Kinshasa provincial health minister banned mayors from issuing opening authorisations and sealed non-compliant pharmacies and health centres in Kalamu 1 on 7 Nov 2024 (infos.cd); ACOREP opened a Kongo-Central division in Jan 2026 and claims exclusive inspection power. No controlled-chemicals/precursor user register found.

coverage.category: 26. Security, cleaning and manpower agencies, and the firms that hire their workers
coverage.found: Found a live enforcement campaign: from 1 Oct 2026 the Vice-PM Interior commission, Protection civile and Police judiciaire inspect guarding (gardiennage) companies in Gombe, Lingwala, Kasa-Vubu and Kintambo, to extend to other communes and provinces (ACP, 2 Oct 2026). Legal basis and exact requirements not stated in the article. See candidate.

coverage.category: 27. Construction, mining and quarry contractors and suppliers: site registers, accreditation, local-content reports
coverage.found: No search spent on ARSP subcontracting or local-content duties (budget used on other categories). Nothing new beyond K03. Mining-side artisanal cooperative items are under category 33.

coverage.category: 28. Notaries, land agents, real estate brokers and other professionals with periodic or anti-money-laundering reports
coverage.found: Two searches. AML law is Loi n° 22/068 of 27 Dec 2022 (replacing 04/016). CENAREF joined Egmont. Could not confirm the list of reporting entities (notaries, real estate agents) or any filing platform or enforcement; a 2024 report calls the system centralised in Kinshasa with limited effectiveness. No DRC real-estate-agent licensing law found. Landlord rent-withholding duty found instead (category 31).

coverage.category: 29. Hotels, guest houses and short-term rentals: guest registers, tourism levies
coverage.found: One search. No DRC text found on hotel classification, guest register or tourist levy; results were other countries. Unverified, nothing buildable.

coverage.category: 30. Small exporters and importers facing traceability or certification rules: food, fish, timber, forest-risk commodities
coverage.found: Timber: artisanal cutting permits (PCA, arrêté 262/2002 and 035/2006) are old; only the second artisanal category may export; no 2024-2027 text found. EUDR for coffee/cocoa: no DRC detail. OCC announced a national QR product-verification system and QR for certified export lots (Sept 2026), obligations not stated. Fish/import side: nothing found (K06/K09 already cover FERI).

coverage.category: 31. Kinshasa provincial taxes on rent and property (DGIPK: rent withholding, property tax, rental income tax, housing allowance, vignette)
coverage.found: The Kinshasa DGRK was dissolved and replaced by the DGIPK (creation order 16 Jun 2026, appointment 28 Aug 2026, transition order 17 Sep 2026). Online filing on e-dgrk.com is required for legal entities and large taxpayers; deadline for September monthly and Q3 2026 rent withholding was 10 Oct 2026. Property tax 2026 was due 2 Feb. See candidate.

coverage.category: 32. Insurance intermediaries and compulsory motor insurance (ARCA, SNECA)
coverage.found: ARCA licenses insurers and intermediaries under Loi 15/005 of 17 Mar 2015 (Code des assurances). SNECA (national digital insurance certificate system, legal basis ministerial order Nov 2022, launched Feb 2023) is a state platform that insurers feed on each contract. Small brokers and general agents exist (a handful of approvals), but the state system covers the core job.

coverage.category: 33. Artisanal mining cooperatives, diggers and comptoirs (SAEMAPE, ZEA, processing entities)
coverage.found: Dec 2025 national suspension of artisanal copper-cobalt processing entities, partly lifted in Lualaba; SAEMAPE identification of cooperatives (31 Jan 2026) and diggers (Apr 2026); ZEA 786 Kasulo launched 14 Jul 2026; South Kivu requires diggers to join recognised cooperatives with joining deadlines. Capmad article blocked (403). Close to K07 (rejected) but a different buyer (cooperative admin).

coverage.category: 34. OCC product certification and QR verification (importers, producers, exporters)
coverage.found: OCC (minister Julien Paluku, 4 Sep 2026) announced a national QR code system to verify products, tied to the 'Système national informatisé de certification aux normes congolaises' presented in Feb 2026; QR for export lots and a holographic-stamp pilot for Made in Congo. Who must comply, legal basis and dates unknown.

coverage.category: 35. Provincial licensing of health and pharmacy establishments (Kinshasa)
coverage.found: Kinshasa provincial ministry took over opening authorisations from mayors, sealed non-viable pharmacies and health centres after a moratorium (Nov 2024), and banned clandestine morgues (Jan 2026). Criteria cited: building, qualified staff, equipment. Unions asked for suspension; outcome unknown. Related to K04.

coverage.category: 36. Inland navigation: boats, barges and pirogues (RVF)
coverage.found: Registration is mandatory for metal-hulled vessels over 20 t and lighter vessels over 50 hp; vessels must be recorded with the river commissioner within a month; RVF collects fees. Source is an old thesis; no 2024-2027 rule found. Mostly out of reach for small non-motorised craft.

coverage.category: 37. Beneficial-ownership and RCCM filings under OHADA
coverage.found: One search. No DRC beneficial-ownership register or deadline found (results were Congo-Brazzaville Law 43-2024 and other countries). One source says a digital national RCCM is being rolled out in DRC. Unverified.

coverage.found: The ARSP regime (law 17/001 of 8 Feb 2017, decree of 1 July 2020, ministerial order 02/CAB/MIN/CMPMEA/2021 of 6 Jan 2021) is active. Registration and renewal are online (formulaire.arsp.cd, renouvellement.arsp.cd). Attestations went electronic with a QR code in June-July 2026; validity rose from 3 to 5 years; target processing time is 7 days. Enforcement is intense in 2026: 408 cement-sector contracts (Apr 2026), KCC/Mutanda 1,540 subcontractors, Ivanhoe subsidiaries 140 contracts (decision 027/ARSP/DG/2026, 30-day corrective plan), SICOMINES, Matadi Gateway Terminal 50 contracts. The 1.2% levy (ex-VAT) is withheld by the main contractor. The 2023 deregistration of 1,203 firms made their contracts void under art. 28. No software competitor found. Mostly K03; two related ledger rows added.

result.competitor: I found no DRC product that tracks SPP compliance (agrément, quarterly reports, CNSS/INPP/ONEM standing). The nearest is the Odoo module l10n_cd_payroll (apps.odoo.com). It calculates IPR/CNSS/INPP/ONEM payroll and produces remittance summaries by collecting agency, so it covers the payroll part of the job but not agrément or quarterly reporting. Foreign contingent-workforce tools have no DRC logic. I found no state SPP portal.
result.duty: Real and in force. Private placement services (SPPs) are governed by articles 303 to 307 of the Labour Code and by ministerial orders on SPP approval. To stay compliant, an SPP needs a valid agrément, or a temporary authorisation if it is less than 2 years old. It must also keep its INPP, ONEM and CNSS standing current and file the required quarterly reports. The Sept 2025 notice gave SPPs 30 working days to file updated dossiers with ONEM. Unlisted SPPs had to report to the ministry by 31 Jan 2026, and an inspection mission started in Feb 2026. In April 2026 the Council of Ministers announced a 30-day moratorium, after which the 402 irregular SPPs would be closed. Penalties are loss of the licence, suspension and prosecution. User companies that use unlisted SPPs commit a 'serious offence' with administrative and criminal sanctions. Not found: the order text, the quarterly report format, the filing channel (probably ONEM, on paper) and any renewal cycle or fees. I found no source confirming that the closures actually happened after May 2026.
result.market: 625 SPPs were inspected. The ministry declared 176 compliant in Jan 2026, and the Council of Ministers counted 223 compliant and 402 irregular in April 2026. If the closures happen, roughly 176 to 223 or more licensed SPPs remain as buyers. User companies are mostly larger mining and industrial firms, which is probably out of scope. The market is very small.
result.reason: The duty is real and enforcement is active (inspections, a list of compliant SPPs, closure of irregular agencies). Nobody offers a dedicated tool for it. But the buyer pool is tiny: about 200 licensed SPPs after the clean-up. The core payroll and remittance work is already covered by generic or Odoo payroll modules, and the remaining work (an agrément file and quarterly reports, probably filed on paper with ONEM) is light. That work suits a consultant or lawyer better than SaaS. The format of the quarterly report is unknown. Willingness to pay among surviving SPPs is plausible but unproven. The user-firm side (list-checking) is a simple lookup and mostly large firms. Low score.

result.competitor: No DRC-specific vendor found. What exists: Congolese academic theses (LUGOZI Security, G.S.A, Bras Security); kolonell.com blog posts on guard planning and time-clock software aimed at Abidjan, Rabat and Casablanca, with no evidence it sells in DRC; and Agenz by Obvious Technologies, a management tool for private security agencies, whose DRC presence is unverified. No state portal found. These tools cover operations (planning, time-clock) rather than the regulatory dossier.
result.duty: Partly confirmed. A 2014 Interior ministerial order (which replaced order no. 98/008) is reported as the regulation in force (AFREWATCH 2021, ICoCA). I could not find its text, so the agrément conditions, renewal frequency and personnel-file requirements are unverified. ACP (2 Oct 2026) confirms Protection civile inspections in Gombe, Lingwala, Kasa-Vubu and Kintambo from 1 Oct 2026, backed by a requisition from the Procureur général of the Cour de cassation. The commission will extend to other communes and then all provinces. Sanctions: non-compliant firms are stripped of staff, agents taken to police, and managers must explain why they operated illegally. The article cites no specific legal article. Working-hours limits under Labour Code art. 189 (Law 16/010) also apply. The fetch of the AFREWATCH PDF returned HTTP 429, so I could not read it.
result.market: Very small. ICoCA says about 100 companies market guarding services in DRC and the regulator recognises about 80 as legal, plus an informal fringe. Some firms are large (Delta Protection claims more than 2,500 agents in Kinshasa). I found no count of Kinshasa firms.
result.reason: The duty partly checks out, but the recurring workflow could not be confirmed. A 2014 Interior ministerial order governs guarding firms (AFREWATCH, ICoCA), but I could not find its text, so the agrément, renewal and personnel-file requirements and their frequency are unverified. The ACP article (2 Oct 2026) confirms inspections by Protection civile with Police judiciaire support from 1 Oct 2026. Sanctions: firms are stripped of staff and agents taken to police. It names no legal basis or documents checked. No DRC-specific software was found. Regional tools exist (kolonell, Agenz), but DRC sales are unverified. The market is tiny: about 100 firms, of which about 80 are legally recognised (ICoCA). Illegal firms are unlikely to pay. Better as a one-off consulting job than recurring SaaS.

result.reason: Duty is real: Law 17/001 and the ARSP regulator. A levy is collected on invoiced amounts. A 2020 report says it was cut from 5% to 1.2%; I found no 2026 rate or filing frequency. In July 2026 ARSP made attestations fully electronic, with remote filing, QR codes and five-year validity. That removes most of the renewal pain, and the free state portal does the registration job. Enforcement exists: about 1,200 firms were struck off, then given a grace period. No private tool turned up. Market size was not found. Buyers are fragmented, informal and poor payers. The levy is probably withheld by principals, so there is little for a tracker to do. Overlap with K03 is likely, and I did not check K03 itself.

Duty partly real: BCC Instruction n°007 (1 Sep 2023) regulates manual exchange (bureaux de change as OHADA companies, cambistes as individuals). On 20 Dec 2025 BCC struck off Force-Unie and told 50 messageries and 62 bureaux to regularise with the supervision directorate or lose approval. But I could not find the instruction text, so recurring registers, reports and AML thresholds are unconfirmed. The Kalieu-Elongo article's licensing details come from the CEMAC framework and do not apply to DRC. The market is small, about 112 named firms, and the one-off regularisation is not a recurring workflow. Willingness to pay is likely low. No competitor or BCC portal was found, but only one search was run on that. Not checked: BCC reporting portal, total licensed population.

Duty is real: DGIPK (ex-DGRK) communiqué sets a 10 Oct 2026 deadline for monthly (Sept) and quarterly (Q3) rent withholding, filed online on e-dgrk.com. It covers legal entities, large individual taxpayers and individuals under five commune directorates. Penalties are only "fines per law", with no amounts. Rates are unverified; a 2009 DGRK document says 20%. The free state portal e-dgrk.com already does the filing, and I found no private helper. Weaknesses: the state portal covers the core job, the buyers are mostly informal landlords with low willingness to pay, the institution is mid-migration so rules may shift, and I found no register count. At best a niche reminder or done-for-you service. I did not check Lubumbashi or Goma.

The duty is real. ARSP decree art. 18 sets a 1.2% levy on subcontract value ex-VAT. The main contractor is the legal payer and the subcontractor the real payer. Art. 18 bis sends 0.2% to a guarantee fund. Payment goes to an ARSP bank account within 15 days of paying the subcontractor, and recovery starts after formal notice. I found no competing product, but this was a thin search. I found no form or filing frequency, and no 2025-26 text confirming the rate. A new content law, Loi 26/018 of 30 June 2026, is being implemented, so rules may shift. Buyers are mid-size main contractors, and the task is a simple 15-day remittance. That makes a standalone product weak. It is a feature to add to a K03 product.
